utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. Before we continue with the current witness, the Chamber would like to address the parties on the matter related to the length of the whole trial. We have now heard the testimony of more than 100 oral witnesses, and we are nearing the end of the Prosecution case. This is a very long trial, and it is the task of the Chamber to ensure that it is fair and expeditious. The Chamber also needs to plan future proceedings as far as possible. This is particularly important given the size of the trial. First of all, the Chamber would like to thank both parties for moving ahead in a generally co-operative spirit during the period of more than one year and three months that has so far elapsed since the trial began. This has certainly been conducive to the expeditious conduct of the proceedings. The Chamber would also like to recall the efforts that it has made to ensure that the Prosecution case is not unduly long and the assistance that it has received from the Prosecution in this regard. On 29 November last year, the Chamber indicated that it considered that the Prosecution case could be completed before the summer recess of 2011. Subsequently, at the request of the Chamber, the Prosecution reviewed its list of oral witnesses and, as a result, made changes which made its case shorter than it otherwise would have been. On the 30th of January and 13th of March, 2011, the Prosecution presented schedules of future witnesses which would allow its case to be completed before the summer recess. The Chamber again thanks the Prosecution for the measures that it has taken to streamline its case. We are now closer to the conclusion of the Prosecution case, and an enormous amount of evidence has been received. The Chamber still believes that it is possible for the Prosecution case to be completed by the 22nd of July, 2011, which is the last day before the summer recess, but this will very probably require further streamlining on the part of the Prosecution. The Chamber stresses that it is for the Prosecution to decide which witnesses to call and how their evidence should be presented in a manner consistent with the Statute and the Rules. But in the interests of an expeditious trial, the Chamber invites the Prosecution to review the witnesses it is intending to call, in light of the mass of testimony that it has already presented, and to consider ways of ensuring that its case does not last any longer than necessary, and that it will use court time in the most efficient way possible; for example, by exploring the possibility of not calling certain witnesses. The Chamber takes the opportunity to invite both parties to consider the appropriate length of their respective examination of the remaining witnesses. This will also have an impact on the length of the trial. Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to make any observations on the matter that I have raised, at the moment or at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. This topic is, of course, one that is of great importance to all of us, and the Prosecution especially, since as it being our last trial, we're planning our lives post-Tribunal. So, in fact, I know Mr. Thayer wanted to tell you this himself, but he has found it necessary to go back to the United States and put his kids in school for September, so his last time here will be up until the recess, July 22nd. And he has to get back to his original job which they've held open for him up until about that time, is my understanding. So we are trying very hard, for many reasons, as well as your encouragement, to finish up our case before the summer recess, including that Mr. Thayer is such a crucial member of the team in that regard, and the organisation, and the co-ordination of witnesses and material. So from that aspect, we have every motivation to do this. And I can tell you that we have now heard from many of the significant Main Staff witnesses, or almost finished with them. We never quite know, as you are aware, if they'll even show up, if people will even show up or be able to show up. We now have remaining General Milovanovic, who is scheduled to be here this weekend to testify next week. I don't think I'm going to take the time that we have allotted. I really hope I'm not. I don't want to be up there that long. And, frankly, we've heard many of the rules and the regulations and the processes and the personalities that are so important for a case like this from some of these other witnesses in a credible way, so I'm hoping to be able to streamline that testimony so it has more meaning for all of us. Then the next -- the big witness, Mr. Butler, who always testifies, and he is our witness that will talk about documents, and intercepts, and areas that may not have been gone into fully, he's scheduled for I believe it's early June, which is on schedule. He's able, as far as I know, to break away from his very busy life in the United States to come here and testify. And I am beginning to organise his materials and try to streamline them so that he is hitting areas that you have not heard over and over again and so that fits into the presentation of the case. The other witnesses, while important, are not lengthy, as far as I recall, and have various important aspects of them. I think we'll probably get back into doing some more 92 ter and that kind of thing. But from the schedule I've looked at, and discussions with Mr. Thayer, who's back at home organising his personal matters, it looks like we're on schedule to finish our case by July. And the question we were asking ourselves and beginning to discuss briefly with Mr. Gajic is the next step, will there be a challenge, a 98 bis challenge. Mr. Gajic says there will be, so we will need to be prepared to provide oral submissions in that matter. And so we're, of course, thinking about when that might happen in relation to the ending of our case. So we're very hopeful that we're going to finish by July 22nd. There's a couple of key areas that have popped up where witnesses -- where a short witness may really help fill a subject matter for you that's important for the case, so you may see a motion for adding a short witness, or 92 bis, or 92 ter witness, very short, but to fill something that has come up that we think we need to fill. And, of course, we'll provide all the justification for that. Ms. Stewart reminds me of one other witness, PW-057, who is another witness that sometimes takes a bit of time, but I don't think he will take too much time this time around. And he is ready to testify as scheduled, which was also in June. So these -- we have, of course, Mr. Petrovic out there, we have the witness that we just lost yesterday. There's going to be some odds and ends, but we're hopeful we're going to be able to finish our case by the break. And when Mr. Thayer gets back - he gets back Thursday - he and I will sit down on Friday and do like what we do, send you out any revised schedule to see where we're ending. But if anything, and maybe I'm being too hopeful, it may be before July 22nd, but I think certainly we're on track for ending our case by July 22nd. And we'll keep everyone informed if there's any changes in any of these more lengthy or critical witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, thank you for this explanation, and this is very helpful for our purposes. You just indicated that you will consult with Mr. Thayer after his return. Perhaps it would be a good idea that you come back to the Chamber and the other party to give us a more specific estimation of the remainder of the Prosecution case after this looking into the details a little more specifically and after consultation with Mr. Thayer. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just something I forgot to add, and I won't spend long. But I can tell you, Mr. President, we have appreciated very much the freedom that you've allowed all of us, in terms of time and witnesses and all. I can tell you, personally, I'm exhausted at this point. And I have a good, strong team, but -- and I think my health has suffered as a result. I don't know why -- this is the first time I've been sick in this Tribunal. In any event, so we're -- and I've spoken to Mr. Gajic. He acknowledges that they're also, of course, feeling the strains of constant trial. And we always need to get ready on the weekend so we can be ready on Monday, because that's when we start, so just as we schedule and as you schedule, please take that into consideration. And, again, we appreciate how much you have in the past and how well you've run this case. We appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Now I should like to move to matters on which the Defence may be -- Mr. Gajic, perhaps you may rise at a later stage. Is it possible or is there a specific need to address something now? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just briefly. The Defence is striving to try to improve the efficiency of the proceedings and not to waste time. I hope we have managed to fulfill the expectations of the Chamber, both in terms of efficiency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, perhaps it's a little bit premature that you raise this at the moment. First, I would like to address the Defence with our questions, and then you may respond to that. That would be very helpful. We would like to move to matters on which the Defence may be in a position to give guidance to the Trial Chamber. I should like to raise the procedure pursuant to Rule 98 bis of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence and the Defence case. Mr. Tolimir, let me stress that you are not obliged at this stage to give any indication as to whether you will be making submissions for the entry of a judgement of acquittal on any of the counts in the indictment pursuant to Rule 98 bis; nor are you obliged to say anything yet about your Defence case. However, as I mentioned earlier, this is a very lengthy trial, and if you are able to provide any guidance on either or both of these two matters, it may assist in the planning of the future of the case. Mr. Tolimir, are you able to say now whether you will be making any submissions in the 98 bis procedure or whether you can give us any indication of the number of witnesses you are intending to call in the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. For the time being, we cannot inform you about the number of the witnesses and the duration of their examination. And as we've heard from Mr. McCloskey, we will only submit regular motions that are part of the normal proceedings. That would be all I can say at this moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey indicated that you were in consultation with the Prosecution, and the Prosecution with the Defence, about a possible 98 bis submission. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, it is an informal discussion between us and, I believe, a normal procedure before this Tribunal. And, of course, yes, we are considering this possibility. Most probably, we will submit a 98 bis motion after the close of the Prosecutor's case. As for the number of witnesses, we cannot provide you any information. We still have proceedings ahead. As you have noted, most of the crucial witnesses are appearing now in the last stage of the OTP case. And on the basis of that, the Defence will make its decision about the number of witnesses, the length of their examination, we will focus on Bar Table motions or bring viva voce witnesses. All these are matters that we are considering at the moment. And, additionally, Mr. McCloskey also mentioned strain that we're experiencing. We're a small team. We don't have any weekends. We're working at full steam. We don't even know what it means to have weekends. We don't know about holidays or anything else. We are completely focused on completing this case as soon as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gajic. The Chamber would appreciate if you could update us, at the specific time when you have reached such a conclusion, to be able to plan the remainder of this case. Thank you for this exchange of views. We should continue with the witness. He should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please sit down. Please sit down, sir. Good afternoon, and welcome back to the courtroom. Mr. Keserovic, I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made at the beginning of your testimony still applies. Mr. McCloskey is continuing his examination-in-chief. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We left off yesterday where you had returned to the bunker at the command post of Crna Rijeka, and shortly after returning sometime that evening, General Mladic gave you an order. And you were describing to us that order, and I think we left off with you describing some of the units that you were to command pursuant to that order. And can you tell us, did you at some point, after receiving that oral order, have you seen a written order reflecting that oral order?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at some time in the more distant future after these events, have you seen an order either in an interview or in one of these court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen it for the first time when Mr. Ruez showed it to me in 2000 during an interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If we could take a look at that. P126.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't -- you didn't bring your documents and your materials today, General?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I - to put it in this way - got the hint and realised that it wasn't necessary to bring anything along.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's not a problem. Sometimes it's better to have documents in front of you than have to work with this screen all the time. But I think I've got most of the documents we've gone over. So can you take a look at this? And we see that it's from the Main Staff, and it's number 03/4. I believe you said that Miletic was going to draft an order, is what Mladic told you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And does this number -- 03/4, do you recall what branch or organ used that number?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then if we go down, we see that it's to the Drina Corps Command for information, and then to various brigades and the Communication Regiment. Is that the Communication Regiment that you had mentioned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We see here that it's the 67th Communications Regiment, but, in any case, that was the communications regiment of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see the first two paragraphs have to do with Zvornik and sending colonels to Zvornik, and you had mentioned that you'd heard General Mladic issue an order about colonels going to Zvornik. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember him saying that Trkulja, Stankovic and Sladojevic should go to Zvornik. I only know that he said they should review the situation and assist with matters that involve co-ordination, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Do those first two paragraphs appear to be related to that order you heard Mladic give to others that night?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's -- let's focus on paragraph 3. And if we could blow that up for the general, because this has to do -- we can see your name mentioned in the middle of it. As we see this paragraph 3, it states that: "At 17 July, the forces of the 1st Bratunac, 1st Milici, the 67th Communication, the Military Police Battalion, the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment and MUP forces are engaged in the wider area of Bratunac, Milici and Drinjaca and will comb the territory in the zone of the Bratunac-Drinjaca-Milici-Besici village, with the aim of discovering and destroying lagging Muslim groups." And then we see it says: "I hereby appoint Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic, the officer for the military police in the Main Staff of the VRS Security Administration, as the commander of all the aforementioned forces during the conduct of the aforementioned task." Then you get a dead-line, and you're supposed to suggest -- make a proposal on the 19th about further engagements. Now, regarding paragraph 3, is that, in your view, related to the oral order you've told us you received from Mladic?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first part of this paragraph relates what General Mladic told me, except I don't remember him mentioning at that time this second part relating to the continuation of the operations towards Cerska. I don't believe he mentioned it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The part you're talking about is that: "An order for further engagement towards Cerska shall be proposed by Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic -- proposed to me by Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic." That's the part you don't recall?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we see the rest of it in English, so Your Honours can just see the next page, so you can see where it's from. And the first page, if we could blow up the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think this is the date stamp that you talked briefly about when you were talking about not being sure about the 17th or the 18th. Could we blow up the date stamp. Okay, we see here that's the 18th of July. And then we see on the next page, it says "18 February." I'm not sure if that's a mistake or just someone thought that "7" was a "2," probably, that was translating it. All right. And, General, we -- because of this slight -- this issue about the date, we managed to look through our records, and we found an original document that appears to have been sent to the Drina Corps. And if we could get the ELMO going to see if that will help us with the time situation. And I want to give you this -- what we believe is an original document, after everybody has a chance to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please go to the first page of this document on the screen at the moment so that we can see the date. There we see it. See the upper left corner, the 17th of July, 1995. Thank you. It may be given to the witness, which means to put on the ELMO. Obviously, we have a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was told that there's a technical problem with the ELMO, and it will be resolved in a couple of minutes. But perhaps you proceed first in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: First of all, General, can you look at this document, and can you tell us, is it the same order that is the one up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should be the same order, except this order was probably sent encrypted by teletype and there's a great number of typos. So it's not the original document from the Main Staff, but it's one of those printed by a teletype, because there's a large rectangular stamp saying "Received/Processed," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the one we have on the computer screen is also a teletype, and it looks like some kind of a received or processing stamp from Milici. So in that regard, they're both received teletyped versions of this order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, seeing how the document is not signed by General Mladic, the one on the screen, it must have also been sent somehow via teletype. I don't -- I can't think of any other reason why it wouldn't be signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Down in the left corner of this original document, we can see, next to Ratko Mladic's name, "S.R." Tell us what that means.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a document is submitted to signalsmen to be sent by teletype or other communication, during the hand-over, because the signature cannot be conveyed by teletype, these letters, "S.R.," meaning "In his own hand," are inserted to indicate that the original document was signed by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. "S.R.," can you just say the Serbian words that "S.R." stands for so I can hear what the Serbian words are?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Svojerucno."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Let's now look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just one moment. Judge Mindua has a question to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, could we see the previous page again in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That means the full page, which is on the screen now. Yes, this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to have this page on the screen. I see that the date marked here is the 17th of July, 1995. In the English version, it says: "Milici, 18th of February, 1995." We have that entry in the English text. I believe this is a mistake, unless we are dealing with two different documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should see the English version, the first page of the English version, please. This is the translation with the same date, 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think His Honour was referring to the second page, where the stamp, under English, says "February." And for some reason, the translator appears to have spelled out the month, when clearly the month was not spelled out in the original. So that is an incorrect way to translate, and I would leave it to the Court to determine -- to me, that looks -- that's a crossed "7," but it could be interpreted as a "2." I think the explanation is the translation just thought it was a "2."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you are right, it's a mistake. The "7" has been translated as "February" here, strangely enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'm told ELMO is alive and well now, so let's try to put this on the screen. And let's start off with the right-hand corner and blow up that handwritten material on the right-hand corner, because we don't have that on the one that's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, looking at that handwritten material in the right-hand corner, we see "OC" underlined. What does that usually mean?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: "OC" usually means "Operations Centre."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you read out to us slowly if you can make out this handwriting under the "OC"?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reads: "Monitor the execution of this task."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of those initials underneath that section?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for Your Honours and everyone, this original document was retrieved from the Drina Corps collection, for your information. Now, can we now just go down and see the bottom of the document, the date stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And before I get to the date stamp: You see that someone has written over in ink in that bottom paragraph. Can you make out why they would have written over in ink like that?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The encryptor who receives a document and finds a lot of typos may add, in his own hand, the correct version, as he understands it. That's one possibility. And the second possibility is that when the end user received this telegram or document, he could, himself, decipher what was meant and then write that clarification down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to this stamp that's at the bottom. And we see this word "Primljeno," and then it looks like -- can you just read that material for us slowly so the interpreters can get what you think that word says and those numbers?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Primljeno," which means "Received," 17 July at 1220 hours. And the signature is of the encrypting officer who received the document. Below that, the number of the telegram, "3671," then something called "Group number" - I don't know exactly what it means - "410." The urgency is indicated as "PP," and again it's followed by some sort of number, "31." Underneath is the processing, which obviously lasted about 10 minutes, and the final document was produced at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So if this document was received by this unit - perhaps the Drina Corps, since that's the collection we got it from, and it was addressed to the Drina Corps, as we saw - does that help you with this -- the issue related to whether you went to this area on the 17th or 18th?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I was informed of that task in the evening, and I was expecting that the order would be then produced by General Miletic, although the document indicates it was written on the 17th of July, and it did arrive, and that's fine, but 17th July, at 12.20, is not in the evening. That could mean that this document had already been prepared, which is less likely, or perhaps it could mean that I was informed of the task in the evening of the 16th. That is more likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you have testified thus far that you were informed of this task or given the order by Mladic on the 16th. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time I either testified or made statements, I said I had not memorised it, but by reviewing some documents and trying to reconstruct events, I arrived at the conclusion I was informed of this task on the 16th and engaged on it on the 17th, although some other documents indicated differently. Based on this document we're looking at, so we could say that I was engaged on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What document are you referring to that suggested differently?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I first saw this document that is on the screen now, it indicates it was written on the 17th of July. I know that I was given that task one evening. That means that -- that would mean that the order was written on the 17th of July, in the evening. I did not have, at the time, this document indicating 12.20 on the 17th of July, which means it had not been received by our unit then. But looking at this and knowing that it was received on the 18th by the brigade, by the Milici Brigade, I simply concluded, based on this document shown to me by Mr. Ruez, that I received the task on the 17th and proceeded with it on the 18th. I was involved in the war for five and a half years, and I cannot remember one particular day, not even a particular month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, in your testimony yesterday, the issue of whether you went to Bratunac on the 17th or 18th was the issue. You were always very clear that you received this order on the 16th. As you sit here now, are you -- when did you receive the order?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let it stand that I received it on the evening of the 16th and went to Bratunac on the 17th. I believe that from all the documents that we have at our disposal, that is the most logical and most realistic option.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll go over some of those documents, for that reason and other reasons. So if we could take the document off the screen for now, and let's just ask you a bit more about what happened that night. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The original document was given back to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we will get this into e-court at 778A so that you have is a copy of this -- oh, it's actually in now, so we can offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 778A shall be assigned Exhibit P2217. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, going back to that evening, and General Mladic issues you that oral order that we're now very clear what it was because we have actually seen this written form, and you testified yesterday that that order concerned you because you didn't think it was realistic, and you also had, I think, some concerns about commanding this group of units, can you tell us what your concern was about being able to go and command these units to do this two-day sweep operation in this particular area?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to command a group of mixed tactical units, it's necessary to set up at least a minimum command base, not necessarily including all that a -- usually organs, but there has to be a command. There has to be a developed command post with all infrastructural elements. There has to be a communications centre, there has to be an operations centre, there must exist the possibility of 24-hour duty service at the command post. And in order to take over command over a unit of a regiment strength in the brigade, all that has to be in place. But the difficulty was I was not the commander of any of the units involved. This could be done by one of the commanders of the units that are covered by the order, and he could then liaise with the other units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, sorry for interrupting. We just have received the other version of the same document, as we see it. That one has no English translation. We have heard from the witness that there are some typos and perhaps other differences and written additions. I think we should only mark it for identification, pending translation. It should be translated as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's a good idea. I'll get one of our good people, so they'll compare both of them to get that correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, General, I -- perhaps it's easy for a lawyer to stand up here and say, You can't always have a command post in wartime, you don't always get everything you need, and I'm sure officers get thrown out and to have to command much worse situations than this, but let me ask you this, in particular: You have described your command experience, both before this and -- I think you took a command, a significant command right after this period, so you were a person with command experience, one of probably a few at the Main Staff at the time; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may not sound modest, but I need to say that I was a good commander. At least that's how I was perceived by the troops and in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you were a lieutenant-colonel then, you're a general now, you went on to be a minister of defence, so I think your army agreed with you. So you were certainly a qualified person to take over command of these units at the time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: My qualification was never an issue. What was an issue were conditions that were in place. If we look from a distance, we can see that the Operation Krivaja took only 10 days to prepare. A command post was set up in Pribicevac. Officers were appointed to arrive. What I'm saying is that it didn't happen that a random group of soldiers was assigned to head towards Srebrenica. That task was feasible. And I always repeat, if somebody had appointed me as the commander of the 1st Milici Light Assault Brigade, together with that brigade and the other brigades in the zone, organise and carry out the task, in that case I would have replaced Milomir Nastic in that command, I would have taken over command, and then I would have been able to work. However, in an open plain, without any support, I was not in a position to carry out that task. I believe that more or less everybody should understand that. I was on my own. There's no single officer who would be able to take over a group of soldiers and take over command over them. It just doesn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Were you aware at the time, the evening of 16 July, that that morning in the Zvornik Brigade, thousands of Bosnian Muslims had over-run, from the rear, Vinko Pandurevic's unit, while at the same time being hit from the 2nd Corps Muslim units from the front, where they lost 40 to 50 men, and Vinko Pandurevic had been returned from the Zepa battle-field on the 15th to deal with that particular situation, leaving the Zepa battle-field in some distress, the Zepa operation having started on the 14th, losing Vinko Pandurevic's assault group on the 15th, Nastic from Milici being up in Zvornik to help Vinko Pandurevic on the 16th with his problems, Vidoje Blagojevic preparing to come to Zepa to take over for Vinko Pandurevic on the night of the 16th, leaving Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic as a person with command responsibility? Were you aware of any of those facts that we have learned in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, I was not aware of any of the details. I was not aware of any of the movements and the participation of the Milici Brigade on the axis towards the Zvornicka Brigade. The only thing that I knew and that I heard from Blagojevic on that day was that he was supposed to head towards Zepa. As for the rest of the information, I didn't know about any of that. I heard about the problems in the Zvornik Brigade somewhat later. I heard that the crowd of some 6.000, 7.000 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't need to know what you heard later. We may get into that, but I just want to do clear something up. You said you heard from Blagojevic that day that he would be going to Zepa. What day are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not on that day. The day after. At that time, that evening, I didn't know anything about the problems that you've just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you heard from Blagojevic the next day, the 17th?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll get to that chronology, but first let me -- you mentioned yesterday that you gave General Mladic some of your concerns verbally while he was there, but he ignored you, and then you, I believe, said you went to General Tolimir. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you see General Tolimir that night?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command post. I believe that he was in the ops room in Crna Rijeka, in the underground command post room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you saw him face to face in the ops room?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, face to face.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there anybody else in the room when you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of officers there. I'm not sure who was listening to our conversation, but I know that Ljubo Obradovic was there for sure. He was colonel at the time, and later on he became general. And Bogdan Sladojevic was also there. He was also a colonel. I'm sure that the two of them were there. General Miletic was also there, but he would leave the ops room to go to his office, and then he would come back. The ops room was in the middle, and all the offices were around it, so people would come and go. I really don't know who was there at the moment, but, in any case, Miletic was there, Obradovic and Sladojevic. I'm sure about the three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tell us what you said to General Tolimir and what, if anything, he said to you.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told General Tolimir -- or, rather, I repeated what General Mladic's intention was. I told him that General Miletic was in the process of drafting up an order in that spirit, and I told him that I simply could not accept that and that I was in no position to carry out a task of that nature. General Tolimir agreed with the way I was thinking, and he told me that he would have a word with General Mladic with regard to the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we observe that you have put this question to the witness yesterday already. I just want to alert you to avoid repetitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'd forgotten that, Mr. President, and I -- it's -- I'll just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you -- and what happened after General Tolimir said that?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, General Tolimir left and went to a different part of the facility, I suppose. I suppose he went to the part where General Mladic was. And he stayed there a few hours, perhaps a couple of hours. I'm not sure how long. After that, when he returned and when I saw him again, he told me -- in one way or another, I'll try to present that. He told me that General Mladic did not relieve me of the obligation to go to the area where the operation was taking place, and the operation was the blocking and the scouring of the terrain, but that I would not be in a position to take over command of units. I would just inspect or tour the zone. I would reach the Bratunac Brigade, and there Colonel Blagojevic would brief me about the course of the implementation of the task, and then I would provide that feedback in the evening. I would brief others that same evening. And he also told me that on that same day, I would have other duties both in Bratunac and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just so it's clear, General Tolimir is the one that's telling you this?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you supposed to come in the evening, and who were you to brief?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following day, I was supposed to come back to the Main Staff and brief them. I should have informed General Mladic about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So if the order was to go there and do this on the 17th, you were supposed to brief General Mladic on the next day, the 18th, or the evening of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I remember about the events, I was supposed to brief him on the 17th, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. What else, if anything, did General Tolimir say to you about any topic?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was supposed to find Colonel Jankovic in Bratunac from the Intelligence Administration, and I was supposed to convey a message to him that a visit should be paid to the Dutch Battalion of UNPROFOR, and that weapons and some other equipment should be returned to them after having been confiscated at the check-points by the Army of Republika Srpska as they were entering Srebrenica. A message was supposed to be conveyed to the DutchBat commander that the plan of the evacuation of the battalion from Srebrenica was changed, that they would not be evacuated via Sarajevo Airport, but rather via Serbia. And I was also to convey a message that the evacuation would be secured by the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska, and Tomo Kovac personally. At that time, Tomo Kovac was either the deputy minister or the minister of the interior. As far as I remember, those were to be my additional tasks and duties. I apologise, there is something else. I'm not sure whether that was a task that I was given. In any case, I was told that Jankovic's obligation would be to supervise the evacuation of the wounded from the Bratunac Hospital, and that evacuation was to be organised by the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall him giving you any other information about anything?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything else. I don't remember any other piece of information that he may have conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember, just roughly, what time of night this was?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps around 9.00 or 10.00, 2200 hours. Sometime between 2200 and 2300 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do after receiving this task from General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went to Crna Rijeka. I went to the barracks, and that's where I spent the rest of that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to show you a few documents for the days before this to see if this is anything you have any knowledge of, or perhaps it will set the scene for us for 17 July. So could we first go to P1605.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, I don't want to spend a lot of time with this, but we can see that it's from a colonel named Ignjat Milanovic. And do you know who he was? Does that name ring a bell to you?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name does ring a bell, but I don't know what the person's duty was. I don't know where he was stationed. I believe that he was a member of the Command of the Drina Corps, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I just -- we can see this is dated 15 July. It's entitled: "Engagement of forces in searching the terrain in the direction of Zepa and the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade ." So it's on that topic again of searching the terrain and it basically, and I'll try to paraphrase it, says that he was ordered to go to the -- Milici and Bratunac and acquaint himself with the situation along the Milici-Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road. And it says: "Generally, large groups of enemy soldiers are still located to the east of this road." And it says: "The 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade is still searching this terrain and is almost at the laid" -- "the limit laid down." Then it talks about the Milici Brigade intercepting groups in the area of Buljim and Susnjari. And it indicates an order he's issued about the general mobilisation to be carried out in Bratunac, Milici, Vlasenica and Sekovici. And then he says: "The assignment you have given to the commander is to be carried out without fail." And then it talks about the order for the Milici brigade and the direction they were going to. And then the Bratunac Brigade was to continue searching the terrain, clearing up the battle-field in the direction of Bratunac-Konjevic Polje-Kasaba. And is that the general area that is later the subject-matter of your search of terrain on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the area, a square between Bratunac and Besici village above Srebrenica-Konjevic Polje-Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then he issues a proposal, and we can see that he's delivered this to the command and to the forward command post, to the attention of the commander. So his proposal is to those commander -- to that commander, and the proposal is "to authorise and appoint the commander of the 1st Bratunac Brigade as commander of all the forces which are participating in searching the terrain and sweeping the battle-field to the east of the road, and in control of the Kasaba-Drinjaca road, because we have no one to appoint from the Command of the Drina Corps." Then on the next page of the English -- sorry, again, I've got a different translation. Sorry about that. It says that: "The Bratunac commander be authorised and appointed a commander of all forces engaged in the search of terrain and clearing up the battle-field" -- sorry, could you raise -- could I get a little more -- I can't read that, and I want to be able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be difficult to have that enlarged, because we have both versions on the screen to enable the witness to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In any event, you can see the proposal for the Bratunac commander to be in command of these units and to conduct this sweep operation, and can you remind us who the Bratunac Brigade commander was at that time?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade commander was Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic. According to what I know -- or, rather, according to the information that I received from General Mladic, he was the one who had organised things to implement that task. He was the one who made it possible for the task to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, and we see this proposal on the 15th. Now let's go to another document, 65 ter 247. Mr. President, so you know, many of these documents were typed and handwritten, and so they ended up being translated by different translators. So the translations get multiple and they get slightly different, but that's -- that's sort of where this problem is created. In any event -- well, we'll get that B/C/S version up for you. If we could get -- there should be a typed version of that so you don't have to struggle with the original hand version. Apparently the typed version is so old that it doesn't show up, so I -- the part I want to read is in the middle of paragraph 2, and I'll just go slowly through this. It's not, I don't think, a contested kind of issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a daily combat report from the Bratunac Brigade, dated 16 July, and we see that it's got a "1640" time written on it at the bottom right-hand corner, and it's to the Command of the Drina Corps. And as you know, these reports give a basic accounting of what's gone on, and the part I want to ask you about is: We see that they're making preparation to dispatch units to the Zvornik Brigade to help, and then it says: "During the day, the brigade commander visited all units which are blocking the enemy retreat (the 1st Milici Brigade, units of the 65th Protection Regiment, parts of the MUP and the 5th Engineering Battalion). Define their tasks and organise their joint action and communications. Because of the engagement of forces of the 1st Bratunac Brigade and the 1st Milici Brigade on other tasks and assignments, execution of the task in searching the terrain has been slowed down, and actions to block enemy forces in the aforementioned area have been hampered." So on the 16th of July in the late afternoon, when this report goes to the Drina Corps, can you tell, from this document, who is in command of those forces doing the terrain sweep and blocking?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see from the report that that person was Colonel Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how can we tell from the report? What -- it doesn't -- does the fact that he is defining their tasks and organising their joint action -- is that an indication of command?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the top of the document, when you go to the very top of the handwritten part of the document, you can see where it says "Command of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade," and the date is the 16 July, and it is a daily combat report. It was only the brigade commander who could send such reports, irrespective of who was in charge of the technical preparations of such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One last question. It's break time, but my question, General, was: The fact that we see here that the commander was defining the tasks of these units and organising their joint action and communication, does that indicate that he's actually in command of all those different units?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that could be an indication, and one could arrive at the conclusion that he did play the role of commander in the entire zone where the operation was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that was, in fact, the proposal of Colonel Milovanovic [sic] the day before, wasn't it, that Blagojevic take command of all these units?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Milanovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And these are many of the same units in the same area that your order was involved in; correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It's a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We must have our first break now, and we will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'd like to tender 65 ter 247, that 16 July daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 247 shall be assigned Exhibit P2218. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, the -- we've left off where I think you've gone back now and you wake up the morning after you receive this order from General Mladic. Tell us what you do.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, I don't know at what hour, I set off from Crna Rijeka or Han Pijesak towards Bratunac. My first stop was at Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was with you, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the driver, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's his name?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Novo Ranitovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And where in Nova Kasaba did you stop?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an intersection where one can make a turn and head for the school, because at the school the Command of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment was deployed. We stopped next to the road, itself, because the commander of the battalion was there at the moment, Major Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time was this did you stop at the headquarters of the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you how late it was. It was maybe 9.00 in the morning, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what, if anything, was said?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it was said that one segment of the Military Police Battalion was active in the area, I was simply briefed by Major Malinic about their activities at the moment and their activities in the preceding days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you, just briefly, say, you know, what you -- what you told Malinic, you know, about your task?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Malinic that I need to go through the zone, get to the zone where the operations were being carried out, and reach the Bratunac Brigade that I was tasked with getting information from Colonel Blagojevic, and that I had some other assignments. I don't know whether I mentioned my other assignments. But, in any case, I told them what my role was that day in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just tell us, briefly, what he reported to you about the situation, what sort of details, as best you can recall? But just outline them. We don't need all the details.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try and tell you all we discussed in the 10 or 15 minutes. The first thing he told me was that he had suspended the training with new troops because there, in the area of the command post at Nova Kasaba, there was only one company that was being trained, a military police company. All other units were outside of that area. So he had suspended the training and deployed that unit, consisting of a hundred to 150 troops, to block the area from Nova Kasaba towards Konjevic Polje, in other words, along the road between those two towns, so they had a line there along that axis. That was the task that the unit was carrying out at the moment, together with Major Malinic. I also received first information about larger groups of POWs being present in the area. They were being transferred. They were on the move from Srebrenica to Tuzla. Major Malinic informed me that late on the 12th of July, but mostly on the 13th of July, there were --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but there's just, I think, a translation issue. We got that there was large groups of POWs that were present in the area and that were being transferred. What did you mean by that, and what dates did he tell you about, if that's what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand you. You mean in my previous answer or at an earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. In the answer you just gave us, it says that you said POWs were being transferred. Is that correct or is that a translation issue?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't correct. On that day, I received first information about POWs appearing in the area in the preceding days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, all right, and I interrupted you. You were talking about the 12th, so go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: So on that occasion, Major Malinic told me that on the night between the 12th and the 13th, and during the 13th of July, there were 2.500 or 3.000 prisoners of war, according to his estimates of POWs, that were located at the football pitch there. He told me that his initial assignment was to register them, which he had started doing, he started registering them, but had to stop doing that because General Mladic told him to stop. General Mladic was passing on that road, and he stopped and addressed the POWs himself. He allegedly told them - he told him as well - that there was no need for registering these people because they were to be transferred/moved to Tuzla because that was their destination anyhow. And Major Malinic then stopped registering the POWs. Immediately after that, or, rather, after some time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Can you tell us what you mean by "registering"?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that lists were to be made, including their names, surnames, name of one of their parents, date of birth, and the place of birth, in other words, basic data for individuals, providing they had their IDs. If they had their IDs, of course, the documents could be used to make the lists. If not, they would be asked to provide their basic data. And the idea was to make the lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you said after that -- you said: "Immediately after that, or, rather, after some time --" And that's when I interrupted you. So what do you remember him telling you next; Malinic, that is?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that he did, indeed, stop making those lists, and that soon after, General Mladic, the commander of the Main Staff, addressed them. Buses arrived to the football pitch in Nova Kasaba, maybe buses and trucks or maybe just buses, and these buses were there in order to transport the POWs to Bratunac. That was done. They entered the vehicles, and under escort, military police escort, Malinic -- Military Police Battalion escort, they were taken to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he mention anything to you about Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did mention -- or Colonel Beara was mentioned there. Allegedly, he either issued or passed on the order for all the POWs to be registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he say where those POWs were to go?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Beara? He did not. I did not hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember Malinic telling you that Beara had ordered that all the prisoners were to be taken to the soccer field?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was the initial order, that they should be located in the area of the football pitch and that they should be registered, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who gave that order to Malinic, according to Malinic?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Beara's order. The way I understood it, it was passed on to him through the duty officer in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Malinic tell you Beara was personally present or did these orders come in over the communications through the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him telling me anything about Beara being there personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this would have come through the duty officer -- from Beara, through the duty officer of the Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, possible. I think -- I think that's the way it was, through the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had General Tolimir told you where Beara was?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point, and as I sit here, I do not recollect when, whether it was on the 16th, in the evening hours, or maybe on the 17th, in the morning, before I departed, I'm not sure about that, but at about that time on the 16th, General Tolimir did say that Colonel Beara was present in the zone of the Drina Corps. I did have that piece of information at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. I just need a clarification from you regarding what you have just stated at page 36, lines 6 to 10. And you've said: "Buses arrived to the football pitch in Nova Kasaba, maybe buses and trucks or maybe just buses, and these buses were there in order to transport the POWs to Bratunac. That was done. They entered the vehicles, and under escort, military police escort, Malinic -- Military Police Battalion escort, they were taken to Bratunac." Were you present when this was happening? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not present. What I'm recounting now is what I'd been told by Major Malinic on the 17th, in the morning, when we ran into each other close to his command post. All the events I'm talking about took place on the 13th, and I was not an eye-witness to the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I -- do you recall, did General Tolimir give you a location in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps? I'm not familiar what's the northern border of their zone of responsibility, because it was neighbouring with East Bosnia Corps, where I had been prior to that. I didn't even know the lines towards the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, but I knew that the command post of the Drina Corps was in Vlasenica. That's the only thing I knew. I don't know any locations and wasn't told about any locations by anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did General Tolimir tell you Beara was located?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere in the zone of the Drina Corps. He didn't tell me precisely where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, and so back to our chronology. Major Malinic is telling you this information. You've added the part about General Tolimir information too. What happened -- what happened after Major Malinic finished telling you this information? Anything else that you recall him telling you?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything else, except for the fact that he told me he'd stay there and continue with his assignment; namely, keeping the communication blocked until further orders. That's the only thing I remember about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I headed on along that road. And after several kilometres between Kasaba and Konjevic Polje, I ran into an officer from the Communications Regiment. I'm not certain who he was, although somewhere in the area the commander of the regiment was supposed to be, but I don't remember having seen him. The officer I saw also told me that the Communications Regiment has one segment of its forces blockading the area facing Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And after checking with that unit, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: From there, I went to the crossroads at Konjevic Polje, and from there to Bratunac. I stopped only briefly at Konjevic Polje because there were many vehicles there, buses, and various members of the army, police. So what they were doing, they were trying to make sure that the traffic would flow faster through the crossroads. And I did not stop there, looking for anyone in charge for that area around Konjevic Polje. And then I went immediately to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslim prisoners assembled around Konjevic Polje or anywhere on this road at this -- at this time?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time, I did not see any prisoners at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about how many buses did you see at the Konjevic Polje intersection?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Perhaps three or four, but there were other vehicles and lorries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you said you went to Bratunac. Where did you go in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I had never been there, I made inquiries, and I went directly to the Command of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, I know you can't be exact, but roughly what time was it when you got to the Command of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was past 10.00 in the morning, sometime between 10.00 and 11.00, not later than a quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did you see there?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked for the commander, Colonel Blagojevic, and I found him on the first floor of the building where the command was based. It was a red building of a factory. And he was alone in his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And describe the -- what was said.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the first time we met. We hadn't met earlier. I told him on what mission I had come to the area; that one of my tasks was to report to him, to be briefed by him as to how the blockade was proceeding and how the sweep operation was proceeding, that aspect of the Krivaja Operation. Blagojevic told me, as far as I remember, that everything was on the move as of the day before, that the units were carrying out the blockade, and the sweep operation was being handled by the units of the police, of the MUP. That's what he said that I can remember. In other words, he had organised all the activities, just as the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he indicate some of his units were involved in that as well?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: His units, or at least a part of his units, was keeping the blockade from Bratunac towards Kravica and Konjevic Polje. Up to what point, I cannot remember exactly, but that was a section of the road between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what else of significance do you recall him telling you?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I recall he said he had already received the so-called preparatory order, and he was about to receive his assignment relating to operations towards Zepa. And part of his forces, together with him, were supposed to head there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can we just go to P1219.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is -- General, it's a log-book that we picked up at the Bratunac Brigade in a search back in 1998. And if we could go to page 10 in the B/C/S, and it should be page -- sorry, page 10 in the English, and perhaps page 10 in the B/C/S. You've got the B/C/S correct. I see that. And, yes, the e-court gods are with us. So we can see in this book, which is entitled "Report on the meetings of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade," that there's a working meeting with the commander, with the corps command. And then the commander -- this is dated the 16th, as we can see, and it says: "The formation of the battalion for Zepa by 0700 hours on 17 July." Is this one of the documents I showed you to help you prepare for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really remember seeing this document. Perhaps I've seen similar documents. Whether it was this one, I'm not sure. But it supports what Blagojevic said, that he was about to prepare and head for Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 3036A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we're waiting: You may remember this is an intercept the Bosnian Muslims were able to get. It's at 1220 hours. If we can find the one in that report that starts at 1220. You're going to have to blow it up to be able to figure that out, I'm afraid. Thank you. That's -- that's it. And this is, I can tell the Court, one of the exhibits that is dated 17 July. If we go to the very top of the report, you'll see the 17 July date, at 1220 hours. Is this an intercept you recall being shown before, I think at a trial a few years back?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and it was shown to me recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what, if anything, are you able to make of this intercept that may or may not relate to this issue we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we are to believe this text, and I suppose we can believe it because this is a transcript of a real conversation, we see that at 12.20, Colonel Blagojevic had already left Bratunac and was on his way, together with his column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My greetings to Mr. McCloskey. Could we see the date on this document? It would be good to see the date; for the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we go back up to the beginning of this report, it should have the date, if we've got the complete thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we do not -- we only put into e-court the section of the report with the -- with the intercept. But for the general, we'll get the whole report. So as I'm sure you remember, to find the date, you've got to go to the top, to the report, and we'll get that so he can take a look at that. But I can assure you it's 17 July, but we can get that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We would appreciate that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall this intercept? I think it was first shown to you as a Defence witness by the Defence attorney for Colonel Blagojevic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And your view, that this intercept that says Blagojevic has set off at the head of a column of seven buses, is consistent with what you've just testified?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe it is. That's what we concluded, that this battalion of the Bratunac Brigade was already moving towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to your chronology, then. You're still in Bratunac. What else do you remember Colonel Blagojevic telling you, besides that he was getting ready to go off to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember talking about anything else with him. We didn't have much time anyway. In the meantime, Colonel Jankovic showed up, and I had been looking for him, so I don't remember discussing anything else in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get to Colonel Jankovic, let me ask you: We'll recall that the original Mladic order, both oral and written, puts you in command of these forces, and then you've said that General Tolimir was able to change that so that you just were to be able to go to the various forces and get information. So now that you see Colonel Blagojevic getting ready to go off to Zepa, what did you do, if anything, about the command situation for the sweep operation?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. As far as I know, nothing, because Blagojevic had his chief of staff, his deputy. I don't know what arrangements he made for his absence, but at that time he had hardly left his area. Srebrenica and Zepa were in the same area. Maybe he never left his own area of responsibility. Anyway, I wasn't even sure he was leaving on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you say Colonel Jankovic showed up. Can you remind us who Colonel Jankovic is?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic was one of the commanding officers in the Intelligence Administration, in the Sector for Intelligence and Security. Now, which section he belonged to exactly, I don't know, but he was used a lot for ensuring communications, contact, and liaison because he spoke English and other languages. In any case, he was in the Intelligence Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you again briefly remind us, had you had a particular assignment regarding Colonel Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already spoken about that. My assignment was to find Colonel Jankovic in Bratunac, and that I did immediately at the command. I told Blagojevic or somebody at the command that I needed Jankovic. Jankovic was found, and he came to Blagojevic's office because I had specific assignments for Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us, briefly, what was said.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was said that he should establish contact with the Dutch Battalion, make apologies somehow for the events that occurred during entry into Srebrenica, when weapons and other assets were taken away from Dutch armed forces, and he was to say that these things would be returned to them. That's one of the assignments I was supposed to convey to him. Another assignment was that he should tell Colonel Karremans, commander of the Dutch Battalion, that his evacuation plan has changed, that it would be done through Serbia and not via Sarajevo Airport, for security reasons. This evacuation would be monitored and supported by the MUP of Republika Srpska; namely, Tomo Kovac. Also, Colonel Jankovic was supposed to arrange somehow the evacuation of the wounded from the Health Centre in Bratunac. That's what I told Jankovic when he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you tell him who he was getting this assignment from?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told him that these assignments were given to me by General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recall what his response, if any, was?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything in particular, because I left the Command of the Bratunac Brigade with him to start carrying out some of these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And tell us where you went and what, if anything, you communicated about.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: After leaving the Bratunac Brigade Command, we went to the Dutch Battalion. At one point, we stopped by the police station in Bratunac. I'm not sure anymore for what reason. Jankovic had some business there. But, anyway, we dropped by. Whether it was before or after visiting the Dutch Battalion, I can't tell anymore, but we stopped by the police station. We went together to the Dutch Battalion Command, where we waited for about half an hour to be received by the commander. We went into his office and stayed there for about an hour. I'm not sure how long it was exactly, but it took some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just briefly describe to us what you did during this hour, or just the topic of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, only vaguely, because Colonel Jankovic spoke in the English language with the UNPROFOR battalion commander, so I did not understand all of it. I didn't understand most of it. I know only what Jankovic kind of interpreted to me in the breaks so that I should be able to follow: that he was telling them what he had to tell them concerning the evacuation, and return of the weapons, and other things that had been taken away. So I wasn't able to follow the entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's just go back for General Tolimir. If we could go to 3036G. That's the big report of that intercept, and we can go to where the date is shown. Okay, there we see the report with the date of 17 July, and, actually, the 12.20 conversation is right up front. So we'll -- and that's 3036G, which we should put into evidence, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you using it with the witness any further?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
