utterances.text: No. I just wanted to respond to the general's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be received, and I think with both versions, one with the date, 17th of July, and the other one, solely the intercept, itself, and the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter documents 3036A and 3036G shall be assigned Exhibit P2219. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. General, let's go back. You've described to us briefly about that you and Colonel Jankovic were carrying out the task that Tolimir had issued for him. And what did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Command of the Dutch Battalion, we went again to Bratunac, and we stopped by the Health Centre, where the evacuation of prisoners was underway, organised by the ICRC. Something was going on there. As we stopped by, somebody - I don't remember who - had separated a group of the wounded, about 20 of them, and these were not evacuated in the organisation of the ICRC, and they eventually stayed there after the column left. And we stayed there and observed until the column of the -- the convoy of the ICRC had left. I remember there was a certain lady, Lucy, organising all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you ever see, that day, a man -- a military man named Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember -- no, I did not know a Momir Nikolic. He was a security officer in the Bratunac Brigade, and I don't remember seeing him on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what did you -- do you know, again roughly, what time the ICRC evacuated those wounded people?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon, around 2.00 p.m., 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do after that? You're still with Colonel Jankovic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we stayed around - how long, I don't remember - after the convoy left. I don't remember at what point we stopped by the police station. After all that was done, we went our different ways. I went back to Crna Rijeka; that is, up the road to Konjevic Polje and Kasaba, towards Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember, while you were in the Bratunac area, did you ever meet with an officer from the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. At the police station in Bratunac, I came across Colonel Ljubisa Borovcanin, who was chief of staff in the Special MUP Brigade, and he was one of the rare officers whom I had known earlier in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why were you at the police station in the first place?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure why Jankovic had to stop by, on what business. But when we went into the police station, in the office of the commander or whoever, there was a large group of policemen, and Borovcanin was with them. I did not have any reason to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Borovcanin say anything? Did you have any discussion or communication with Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said some things we spoke about, what he did, and he said he was there with some of his forces. And he said that his forces were mixed, that he had some members of the Special Brigade and some police officers from the rank of regular police forces from various police stations. From the Zvornik Security Services Centre, that encompasses Bratunac and Milici. Those were special units, in other words. He also said that those special units were deployed in some check-points, including Konjevic Polje, but all of his troops were mostly engaged in scouring the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "scouring the terrain," was the "search of the terrain" job that was the subject of your earlier order by General Mladic, or similar to?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's the search Colonel Blagojevic was talking about when he said the troops were blockaded and that the police would be sent out to search the terrain. So, yes, that's the task I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. At page 47, lines 23 to 25, through to 48, lines 1 to 3, you have stated as follows: "Something was going on there. As we stopped by, somebody - I don't remember who - had separated a group of wounded, about 20 of them, and these were not evacuated in the organisation of the ICRC ...," and so on and so forth. ^ Then you come to say: "I remember there was a certain lady, Lucy, organising all that." My question is: From which side of those involved in that evacuation was Lucy from; the ICRC, or the MUP, or another organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ICRC, they brought vehicles and they carried out the evacuation. So it was the International Red Cross that did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: And so Lucy, the lady Lucy, was from the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And perhaps on that same subject: Do you know why those 20 were separated that didn't get transported?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were stories, people talked, and it was said that those combatants had been identified as perpetrators of crimes that happened during the previous period and that they couldn't be evacuated together with the rest. That was the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did the separating of these 20 individuals from the larger group that was evacuated?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it the ICRC that separated them?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. Madam Lucy actually fought hard for everybody to be evacuated, without any selection or separation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. And this information, you say "stories," where did that come from?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all the stories were heard there within the perimeter of the Health Centre, and most of the people who were there were police officers probably from Bratunac. I don't know if there were members of the military too. I didn't notice anybody but Jankovic, and, of course, I myself was there. And there was also doctors, medical staff from the hospital. They all made up a group that talked very agitatedly about the problem, and that was the first time the issue was raised about that group that couldn't go. Who identified them and who issued an order for them to stay behind instead of being evacuated, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And on a related topic: Did you deal with any issues with an international group called Doctors Without Borders, MSF?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Doctors Without Borders, I know who they are. My only personal contact with them was when I met them as members of a mobile hospital in Banja Luka. After I was wounded, I asked them for medical assistance. Otherwise, I did not have much to do with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to where you were talking with Mr. Borovcanin about the sweep operation: Did you come to any decisions about the sweep operation with the army and his forces or anything of significance?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I just took stock of the situation. I had some personal contacts that helped me with that, and I also relied on what Blagojevic and Borovcanin told me. I realised that the operation was ongoing, that it was underway, and that it would come to an end pretty soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Could we have 65 ter 1435.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, I don't want to spend too much time with this. I'm not sure you've seen this before, but I just want to ask you if you have. It's a 17 July order from a Special Police commander named Goran Saric, and as we can see, it's sent to a group of people, including Ljubisa Borovcanin, the person you just mentioned, and the Bratunac Public Security Station, where -- is that where you were talking to Ljubisa Borovcanin, at the Bratunac Public Security Station? --

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see, in paragraph 1 of this, that it talks about forming a combat group on the 17th to search the terrain of the Pobudje sector and clear the side of the Milici-Drinjaca road. Is that basically this part of the sweep operation that you were sent down to co-ordinate and be involved in to some degree?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was one part of the operation. But as I've already told you, I was not supposed to take an active part in it in that way. I was just to see how things were going on. I was just sent out to be there and to see how things were done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Understood. Have you ever seen this order before?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1435 shall be assigned Exhibit P2220. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And going back to your chronology: Before I'd asked you about the Special Police, I think you'd basically gotten yourself -- you had split up with Colonel Jankovic, and you'd started going back to Crna Rijeka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: After all of the activities in Bratunac, namely, the evacuation of the wounded, I visited the police station and to the DutchBat. When everything was finished, we went our separate ways. During that period of time, Colonel Jankovic actually stayed in Bratunac. He never told me that; not in so many words, but that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he give you any messages to pass on to anyone at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special. The only thing that he told me was that he had accomplished his mission with the Dutch Battalion, and then we agreed that I would say that some of the prisoners had stayed behind in the Health Centre; that some of them were not evacuated, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And about what time did you leave the Bratunac area?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, sometime after 1600 or 1700 hours. It was still daylight. It was summer, summertime, and the visibility was good. I would say sometime late in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you stop anywhere along the way home towards Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that we stopped. I remember that we had to stop before Konjevic Polje for 10 or 15 minutes because the road was blocked with vehicles which were making U-turns in that area. That's what stopped me for 10 minutes or so on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an occasional bus, but mostly lorries, some all-terrain vehicles. I believe that on the side of the road, I even saw an APC on the road to Drinjaca, where the road forks off towards Drinjaca. I believe that even APCs were there. There was some -- there were a lot of passenger vehicles. I really can't tell you exactly what I saw, what kind of vehicles I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Whose APC was this?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, I don't understand. No, I didn't say "transport." I never mentioned any transporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have, in the English translation, that: "I even saw an APC." An armoured personnel carrier is what that's short for. Did you ever say you saw an armoured personnel carrier?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I said that it was a piece of engineering machinery, a piece of machinery or vehicle belonging to engineers. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of machinery? What was the machinery designed to do?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a classical dozer -- bulldozer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was it a machine that could dig?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a combined piece of equipment. It could dig and it could also push the earth in front of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you see any Muslims around, any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why were these vehicles turning around, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why. They were moving in all sorts of directions from there; towards Bratunac, Kasaba, and towards Drinjaca. In any case, at one point in time that crossroads was totally blocked. I don't know why all the commotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And after that delay, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back to Crna Rijeka, to Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did you see back there? Actually, let me ask you: Roughly, what time did you get back to Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At sunset, around 1900 or 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did you see back at the Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I went to the Operations Centre, where General Miletic was. I don't remember who else was there at the time. I briefed General Miletic about the search of the terrain. I don't know how much time I spent with him, and I really don't remember whether our discussion touched upon any other topics. I can't remember that. After that, I went down to the barracks, or, rather, to the command post. And there, over a period of a few hours, I conveyed the same information to General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, roughly, what time of day was it? If you got back at about sunset and you went to the Operations Centre -- actually, let me ask you: When you went to the Operations Centre, was that the one in the bunker or the one in the buildings?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Operations Centre in the bunker. And everything happened within the scope of a few hours, so I wouldn't be able to pin-point the times exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so you leave the bunker, and you go see General Tolimir where?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the prefabricated buildings, in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you say to him?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like in the Operations Centre, but I also told him about the tasks that we carried out together with Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And those are all -- those are the tasks that you've already told us about?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything special. Perhaps we said a few things, and he said that the separation of some of the wounded was not okay and that that situation had to be resolved over the next few days. I vaguely remember something to that effect. And after that, we discussed the upcoming tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what were those? Tell us about what you discussed with him.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we discussed things to do over the next few days. For example, on the following day or over the next two days, I was supposed to talk to the officers of the military police who had completed training in the Army of Yugoslavia and who had joined the Army of the Republika Srpska, and I was supposed to give a proposal to the commander as to how they would be deployed. After that, I was supposed to go to the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and there I was supposed to meet with the officers of the Security Department of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I was supposed to take stock of the situation over there, in view of the all-out offensive which was launched from Sarajevo against the axis from Trnovo to Kijevo. That axis had been threatened at the time. Most of the Battalion of the Military Police and the Protective Regiment were deployed on that axis. As for the other tasks, I was supposed to have a meeting and a conversation with the group of Russian volunteers. I was supposed to brief them about the rules of engagement. They had turned up with an intention to be deployed in the Sarajevo front-line. Another task was for me to talk to a group of officers that had been selected to replenish the security organs in the units where those were missing. All those things were supposed to be done over the next four or five days, before the 23rd of July. And on that day, I travelled to Drvar, to the forward command post of the Main Staff, where I joined the general, General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And who told you about all these tasks? Who told you you were supposed to do all these things you've just described?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir, General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember telling us before about going to Sarajevo to bring an officer from an international organisation to take part in some agreement with Mladic in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: When General Tolimir gave me the list of tasks facing the Security Administration or, rather, the Sector for Intelligence and Security, all in the function of the intention for me not to take over command of those units. He mentioned, amongst other things, that a military mission in Sarajevo was supposed to send a certain Colonel Howard and another officer, or, rather, that they should have been brought over to monitor negotiations between the VRS and the leadership of Zepa. However, I did not carry out that task. I don't know why. I must have forgotten it. As far as my memory serves me, that task was actually never issued to me, and there is nothing that would tell me that it ever was. There are no notes to that effect or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did General Tolimir tell you about this task of getting Colonel Howard?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentioned that task in the evening on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And those other tasks that you -- that he gave you when you got back from the Bratunac area, were those in written form, or oral, or both?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oral, those tasks were conveyed in an oral form. That was a customary way of communication among the security officers or, rather, the officers in the Security and Intelligence Sector. The only exception would have been engagements that dealt with things that were not within the normal scope of our activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, General. It's break time. And, Mr. President, I have just a couple of documents to clear up some of the timing issues, but I'm hoping 15 or 20 minutes is all I have left. And given that I've been on for five hours and forty-five minutes, I better not have more than fifteen minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told you have only used five hours and forty-three minutes. That means you have really a quarter of an hour left. We must have our second break now, and we'll resume at quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I want to go over a couple of documents. I think you've seen them sort of briefly. If we could go to P00376A. And this is an intercept, and I can tell you that it's from 17 July 1995. I think -- you've seen it before, I know. It's got your name in it, and it's between X and Y. And we can see that it talks about: "Has Keserovic set out already?" And X says: "We came across him on our way here." It's 11.15 a.m. on the 17th of July, and it's hard to make out exactly what they're talking about, but have you seen this intercept before?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, in the printed version, typed version of it, of this issue where I was, because I was expected somewhere in the area on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the typed version is B, if we can show that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that it mentions at some point: "Well, he must have gone first forward over there to Momir Nikolic." We know that Momir Nikolic was in the Bratunac area. During this period of time after you got back to Eastern Bosnia, the 16th, 17th, 18th, did you ever go to the Bratunac area but once, that you've told us about, or did you ever go there again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast. I was told it is a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was in Bratunac only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would tender this document -- it's already in, I see. It's got a P number. All right. Let's go to P1747, and it should be page 4 in the English and page -- I've got "89" in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a log-book from the Zvornik Brigade, and this is a log-book for 17 July. Do you remember me showing you this 17 July entry?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and also that at 0845 hours, three colonels showed up in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And it's mentioning "led by Colonel Trkulja," that they went to the IKM to review the conditions and then returned at 1500. Does this assignment led by Trkulja, does that -- is that related to anything that you heard General Mladic order anybody else to do on that 16th?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is related. The three colonels, that's what we saw in items 1 and 2 of the order. They were told to go to the Zvornik Brigade, and to assess the situation there and to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And so if this is correct, they would have left Crna Rijeka probably in the morning and driven there, or do you know if they went to Zvornik and spent the night before going out to the IKM?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with their time of departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, General, I want to ask you a couple of final questions. You've told us that you were not in command of the sweep-up operation, but I want to tell you there's a witness in this case that has testified he was one of the officers for the Special Police, under Mr. Borovcanin, and he said he was involved in the sweep operation - and this is at page 8633 of the testimony - on the 17th of July, and that by the end of that sweep operation that he conducted with the army, they had received about 200 prisoners. And there are indications in this case that some of those people turned up in a mass grave in Cerska, and certainly 200 people from the 17th have never been seen again. So, General, I'm concerned that you have said that you were not in command of that sweep operation because you're aware that prisoners were captured and then killed at the end of it. Is that true? Were you in command of this sweep operation?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you first find out that Muslims were summarily executed by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: People started talking about it just before the end of the war, but I didn't have any concrete information before the first trials to Erdemovic and Kremovic here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you say near the end of the war, what month are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be precise about that. But, in any case, semi- and unofficial information started appearing in newspaper articles, rumours, to the effect that something had happened and that humanitarian organisations are trying to locate people from Srebrenica. But nobody in Republika Srpska officially and publicly spoke about that. I didn't have any information about it, and I wasn't in the area until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we have the page on the screen, 8633, but we can't see that there is a reference to testimony about these events by the military police. Can you check that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hadn't meant for it to come up, but it's -- I just wanted to ask him about it. And I realised that this was testimony that's part of the record of this case at 92 bis, but it's actually testimony from the Popovic case. So it's not our -- that's the reference for where it's in evidence, but I probably need some more numbers for you to bring it up in this case. And it wasn't my intention to do that. I don't think they'll be any disagreement that that fundamentally was testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was very helpful to have it on the screen. Otherwise, later on we all would have trouble to find the right location. That may be checked later. Just continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's PW-052, 92 bis, and that is the correct page from Popovic. And that was my last question. Thank you for clarifying that for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take it you concluded your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it's now your turn to commence your cross-examination. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace reign in this house, and may God's will, not mine, be done in these proceedings. My greetings to Mr. McCloskey. We are all pleased that he's back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My greetings to Mr. Keserovic as well. I would like to congratulate him for all his accomplishments. Last time I saw him, he was a lieutenant-colonel in the VRS. In the meantime, he has become a general and has obtained his doctorate, so my congratulations.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We don't have much time, Mr. Keserovic, maybe 20 minutes at the most, and we'll try to go back through the transcript to remind you of some of the discussions before my turn came. But, please, before you answer, wait for the transcript to stop so that we wouldn't overlap. On several occasions during the previous session, you were asked about your stay in Bratunac together with Colonel Jankovic. For instance, on page 44, line 21, you said: "Jankovic spoke English, and he was a member of the Intelligence Administration. He was used for interpretation because he could speak two different languages." Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was everyone in the administration aware of the fact that Jankovic was there only to interpret, and that he was summoned to Srebrenica precisely for that purpose; namely, just to be an interpreter? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that Jankovic was used as an interpreter, and that is why I was not aware what his precise role was within the Intelligence Administration besides that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now look at document 03884, and this document will help us understand why the knowledge of various languages is of use for the Intelligence Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: There is a document on the screen now that was sent by the Intelligence Administration to the Sections for Intelligence Affairs of the Herzegovina Corps, Drina Corps, and to the Organ for Intelligence and Security Affairs of the IKM of the Herzegovina and Drina Corps. It is stated here: "Activities of the NATO Air Force." And it says at 1344 hours, AWACS called two American aeroplanes, F-18, with code-name Thebault ^ 37, to fly over Gorazde, fly over the Gorazde, and record the situation there. And later on, they were asked to fly over Serbian positions at supersonic speed and to be in touch with the British VON, code-name Fortune 95. But until they come to that location, to stay in contact with them. I apologise to the interpreters. So this is mention of a situation where it was necessary to translate communication between the aeroplane and the station. Do you remember who in the administration was in charge of translating such documents when they would reach us with written in English on them?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think Captain or Major Mamlic also spoke a foreign language. Jankovic also knew some foreign language. And was there anyone else we used to translate for us? I'm not able to recall at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you mostly convey to Jankovic assignments that were related to UNPROFOR, UNPROFOR, ICRC, and so on, which were a part of the duties of our administrations because we were the ones who were in contact with international factors and representatives?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively such assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were all your contacts with Jankovic in Bratunac in relation to activities regarding UNPROFOR and UNHCR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey asked you on several occasions whether you conveyed Tolimir's orders. My question is this: Were those orders or were those tasks pertaining to the regular work of the organs in the sector? Were those military tasks, military orders, or were those regular tasks?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were regular tasks. Those that are carried out in the Intelligence and Security Sector, those were not military orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked, on page 56, about the tasks you received, and you listed them. For example, you mentioned the deployment of newly-admitted officers who had just arrived from training. You also spoke about the deployment of new security organs. You mentioned talks with the Russian volunteers. All that we can find on page 56, starting with line 17. And you said that you were to carry out those tasks from the 18th, when you returned from Bratunac, up to the 23rd, when you went to Drvar on a new assignment. Is there a single military task among these? You also mentioned the fact that two monitors were supposed to arrive to supervise negotiations between the VRS and Zepa. Would you say that any of these tasks is a military task?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is nothing outside of the purview of the normal work of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you are familiar with the Rules of Service, would you say that there is anywhere in the rules a ban on communications between officers and those employed in the Security Sector? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no such thing in the rules, there's no ban on communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All of those tasks that you carried out together with Jankovic, the tasks you carried out after your arrival from Bratunac until the moment you left and went to Drvar, were they all within the purview of the work of the security organs, and were they all part of their professional duties? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all professional tasks.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the Pre-Trial Chamber [as interpreted] admit this document into evidence, the one that we have just called up on e-court? Thank you. And then we will continue when Mr. McCloskey has had his say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We received the interpretation "Pre-Trial Chamber." There is no Pre-Trial Chamber at the moment. It is the Trial Chamber. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. It may be a translation issue, but we're getting a distinction between tasks, kind of regular tasks, and military tasks. And so, foundationally, if the general and the witness could establish what they mean by that, it could have some meaning, but in English it has no meaning because these are all the military men and everything is a military task in that sense. So unless foundationally you establish what you mean, it has no meaning. And, again, it's probably translation, but I just want to point that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's not the first time that this question occurs here in this trial. First, we will mark this document on the screen for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 3884 shall be assigned Exhibit D247, marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have heard the desire of Mr. McCloskey. You may clarify that or not. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to thank Mr. McCloskey for having corrected my mistake. I said "Pre-Trial Chamber." It was not the interpreter who made the mistake. And now I'm going to ask Mr. Keserovic, and maybe he can clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, when a commander, in keeping with his own decision or his own design, issues a task to all of us, are security organs or members of the Security Sector duty-bound to work on the implementation of such tasks? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are duty-bound to do that. Everybody has to carry out the commander's tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were we all subordinated to all those who were in command positions in the commands of the brigades, corps, main staffs? Did we report to them about our own work along the command line, along the line of the chain of command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we reported to the members of the command, to the assistant commanders, depending on where we worked, and we were responsible for our overall work before the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On several occasions, you asked whether I changed the commander's order. I don't want to quote, but if necessary, I will provide references. My question is this: Did I change the commander's decision or was it the commander, himself, who changed his decision before you set out to carry out the tasks that he had given you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not change the task or the order. I believe that that's what I said. You conveyed the message to me, and you told me that the commander, himself, had changed the task before I went on the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. You were asked on page 44, line 7, about that, but I didn't want to mention either the page or the line before you answered. My next question is this: Did anybody, any of the organs, including the chief of the Sector for Intelligence and Security, have the right to issue any tasks or orders to the organs who were not on the strength of either the sector or the administration?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I didn't understand your question. You say "task." I didn't understand your question. In professional terms and in terms of professional control of counter-intelligence, if that is what you meant, one could issue tasks from the sector and Administration for Security to the Security Department, but those could not be military tasks or orders, nor could security organs be taken out from the chain of command in the unit that they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you performed different duties, starting with the platoon commander to your last position - you were also a corps commander and chief - can you tell us this: If any other organ issued a command to any organ of the command, would you request clarification? Would you seek to find out why that order had been issued unbeknownst to you?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The relationship in the command is indivisible. The commander is the only one that can issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to professional bodies or organs, did they have the right only to issue tasks to their own professional organs at various levels or did they have the right to issue tasks and orders to the commanders and their units?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could issue orders and tasks only to their own professional organs. They certainly couldn't issue orders to units, and that applied to all organs, not only to security organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Keserovic. Please, if you did not carry out a task given to you by the commander, would you be taken to task by myself or by the commander? For example, just to illustrate the situation, when you were sent to Bratunac to carry out the mission, who were you responsible to?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And would you have been taken to task by me if you had not carried out my task; for example, if you had not briefed Jankovic about the tasks that I had given you?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have been taken to task first by you and then by the commander, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For grave breaches of discipline, for non-compliance with orders, which disciplinary bodies are authorised? Do security organs report only to their professional superiors or do they also have to bear responsibility before courts?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: They bear responsibility before military and disciplinary courts, civil courts, and commanders are command organs; wardens, chiefs and organs of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as tasks, obligations and status issues of officers in intelligence and security organs are concerned, is it the chief of the sector who is in charge or is it true that some of them have to be dealt with by the commander?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: All status issues are dealt with by the commander or the authorised body is of the command. Proposals may be given by the sector; in other words, the chief of the sector or the chief of the relevant administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. I believe that we have clarified the issue that was raised by Mr. McCloskey. If we have not been successful, we can go on exploring the issue. Maybe we can leave it to Mr. McCloskey to raise the issue again in his redirect. Thank you for your answers, in any case. Please, on page 22 of today's transcript, on line 6, you were asked whether on the 16th of July, you knew that the unit of the BiH Army had left Srebrenica and that it had walked over the Zvornik Brigade, and that Blagojevic was supposed to go to Zepa on the day when you were with him in Bratunac. Do you remember that, and could you understand the question, since you speak English?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, can you answer the following question: What forces walked over, as the Prosecution put it, the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, they over-run that area of responsibility, and where did they open fire from against the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it got cleared up right at the end, but the term has been translated as "walked over," and I believe I probably used the term "over-ran," which the translator got to eventually. But I think everyone agrees that it's "over-ran" is the appropriate term in English, not -- well, "walked over" is another way of saying it, but not a military way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I remember very well that you used the word "over-run," and, indeed, Mr. Tolimir used it as well. Your answer, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know today about what happened at the time. That evening, I didn't know, I didn't have that information. However, I know today, according to estimates, some 7.000 or 8.000 people from Srebrenica, from the 28th Division, and perhaps a few civilians together with them, hit the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade. They attacked from the rear. They inflicted major losses on them. And the commander of the brigade decided to open the corridor to let them through towards Tuzla, towards the zone of the 2nd Corps, because he simply could not engage in combat with them because they were simply more powerful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was that prevalence in power in terms of the numerical strength or also the technical strength? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, it was mostly the numerical strength of that division. They had some infantry weapons that they could carry. However, as they were encountering the elements of combat order of the Zvornik Brigade, like artillery and orders, they would get hold of those and turned the barrels against the Zvornik Brigade. However, I would say that the numerical element was prevalent in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Keserovic. As a soldier, would you be able to analyse the military activity of the Muslim forces that had left Srebrenica? How would you term those activities?

utterances.speaker: Dragomir Keserovic [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, we are talking about a forcible march. That would be the correct military terminology, and that would imply a movement involving the use of all available means. And in the final part, the activity was an offensive from the rear against the Zvornik Brigade and the Drina Corps, and those activities were in the direction of the 2nd Brigade of -- or 2nd Corps of the BiH.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at D176.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for it, I would like to say that this is a document which was issued by the BiH Army, the Command of its 2nd Corps, on the 27th of July, 1995, and the title is "The chronology of the breakthrough of the 28th Division." It was sent to General Rasim Delic. The commander of that brigade was Sead Delic. Do you see the document now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, excuse me. I just see that it's getting late, and I don't have an estimate for cross-examination. And we need to know tonight if we need to get ready for anything tomorrow, so if, before we quit, we could get that estimate, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will finish whenever you tell me to finish, but not this evening. I can't finish within the next 15 minutes. I have a lot of questions, I have a lot to deal with. There have been a lot of questions put to the witness over the past two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, that was not the question. We will finish at 7.00 today, and it's very clear -- it's obvious that you can't finish your cross-examination in the next two minutes. You have indicated earlier that you will use three hours for cross-examination. Can you give us an update, as the Prosecution used more than the estimated three hours at the beginning? What is your estimation for the whole of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Through our contacts with the Registry, we said that we would need as much time as the Prosecutor has used. If you don't mind, we would like to use that right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You always should use your right. It was just a question by Mr. McCloskey and by me. That means six hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approximately, approximately six hours. I'll try to finish even before that. I'll try and make sure that I leave some time within my six hours for redirect, for additional questions by the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Taking into account this information, it is very clear that we will not finish with the witness by tomorrow. We will go further into the next week, I think. After we have had this discussion, there is no reason for continuation of cross-examination. We should adjourn for the day. You should be reminded, sir, there's no permission to have contact with either party about the content of your examination. We adjourn, and we resume tomorrow afternoon at 2.15 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of May, 2011, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
